title: Repair
hookLine: a moonlit grove, a frightened king, and the Buddha's three-part answer to a confession
tomorrow: why would a young man bow to the east for his parents?

lines: A FULL MOON, A MANGO GROVE.
cards: Some apologies sit in the versions folder for days. This one waited much longer. A full moon.

A king named Ajatasattu rides toward a mango grove at night, guided by his physician, Jivaka. The Buddha is there, they say, with a great gathering of monks. But as the king gets close, the grove is silent.
No coughs, no voices, nothing. His hair stands on end. Jivaka, are you leading me into a trap?
Jivaka points: look, the lamps are lit in the hall. The king walks in, and finds the monks sitting perfectly still, like a clear lake.

teach.b: The king asks his question about the fruits of a monk's life, and listens to a long answer. Then he goes for refuge. And before he leaves, he says the thing he came carrying.
A fault overcame me, foolish and confused as I was. For the sake of the throne, I took the life of my father, a good man and a good king.

May the Blessed One accept my fault as a fault, so I can restrain myself in the future. A word for parents listening with children: this is a hard confession, and the Buddha doesn't pretend it's small.
Yes, he says, a fault overcame you.
But because you see it as a fault, and make amends in the right way, we accept it.
And then the line that carries the whole story: it is growth, in the discipline of the noble ones, when someone sees a fault as a fault, makes amends, and holds back in the future. Three moves.
See it plainly, no softening. Make it right, as far as it can be made right. And don't repeat it.
Notice what's missing: a lecture, a long punishment, a demand to grovel. The deed isn't erased. A father is still gone, and the king will live with that.
But the growth starts the moment it's named, and every day it stays unnamed is a day it doesn't.

how: Buddhist monastics confess faults to one another as part of their discipline, and many lay Buddhists bring the same three steps (seeing a fault, making amends, resolving restraint) into family life.

o: paying a fine to a monastery for a broken rule
a ritual washing that removes past bad karma
naming a fault, making amends, and holding back after

games.q: the king's night in the grove — tap the pairs.
p: the physician who led the king there
see it, make amends, hold back after

s: the Buddha told the king his deed was wiped away
he accepted the confession and called it growth; he never said the deed was undone.
the king grew afraid because the grove full of monks was silent
he asked Jivaka if he was being led into a trap, until he saw the lamps lit.
in the story, a real apology has to come with a long penance
the Buddha names three moves: see the fault as a fault, make amends, hold back in future.

games.q: you're the king. you've heard the teaching and gone for refuge. the thing you did is still unsaid. what do you do?
o: name it plainly, ask that it be accepted as a fault, and promise restraint.
leave quietly; the refuge already covers it, and naming it would only hurt.
explain the politics first, so the Buddha understands why it had to happen.
games.why: Ajatasattu says it plainly, calls it a fault, and asks for acceptance for the sake of restraint. the Buddha accepts it and calls that growth.

practice: If paper is nearby, write one sentence of apology you owe someone, plain and short, with no 'but' in it. If not, shape it in your mind, word by word. Read it back once, slowly, and notice whether your shoulders change.
Then let it be ready for the right time.

wordCard.voice: Repair: seeing a fault as a fault, making amends, and holding back after. The king's three moves, accepted in a moonlit grove.

orig.note: Pali: a fault or transgression; the king says a fault 'overcame' him.

carryVoice: A line for the road: repair quickly, because the growth starts when it's named. Four of four, and speech at home is closed.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 2 (Samaññaphala Sutta: Ajatasattu's full-moon visit to Jivaka's mango grove; his fear at the silence; the monks still like a clear lake; his confession of killing his father for the throne; the Buddha's acceptance: seeing a transgression as such, making amends according to the Dhamma, and undertaking restraint is growth in the noble one's discipline)
